title: Collection Escape Hatch
user: An API developer moving a team off Postman who needs to prove that collections, environments, auth, scripts, and examples survived the move before changing the team's daily client.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Asks for Postman alternatives; replies immediately enumerate Kreya, HTTPie, Bruno, and curl, showing fragmented replacement workflows rather than a safe migration path.
A user reports that a large Postman collection cannot be imported into Hoppscotch, a concrete portability failure after choosing an alternative.

recurrence: At least two independent 2025 askers, plus a long-running ecosystem of importer bugs; migration is high-stakes because a silent loss of auth/scripts breaks team workflows.
current_workaround: Try several clients, import a copy, manually spot-check requests, or fall back to curl and hand-maintained files.
incumbents_and_gap: Bruno, Hoppscotch, Insomnia, Kreya, and Postman each import some formats. None is a neutral local verifier that produces a field-level loss report and a repeatable migration fixture across clients.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that reads Postman v2.1 plus one target export (initially Bruno/Hoppscotch), checks requests, folders, variables, auth, scripts, examples, and body sizes, then emits a Markdown/JSON migration report. Non-goals: another API client, cloud sync, or executing production requests.
success_measure: In 10 imported real-world collections, users find every unsupported or changed construct before switching clients; at least 70% of report recipients run it again in CI or a release checklist.
constraints: Must run fully locally; redact secret values while preserving variable names and structure; track Postman and target-format licenses and schemas.
why_distinct: It validates a migration between API clients instead of competing to be the API client.

title: Internal Event Ledger
user: A solo developer or small product team that needs to review non-urgent operational events without letting them disappear inside Slack channels.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker routes product, backend, and third-party webhooks to Slack but says the feeds are noisy, hard to search/filter, and cause missed events; Sentry and PagerDuty feel excessive.
A Sentry user asks for Slack alert threading without also sending every alert to the channel, documenting the channel-noise problem even in a mature incident tool.

recurrence: Independent small-team request plus a product issue in a major error-monitoring project; severity is moderate but chronic because important status signals get mixed with chat.
current_workaround: Dedicated Slack channels, email, Notion/Airtable, or an expensive observability product with alert rules.
incumbents_and_gap: Slack, Sentry, PagerDuty, Better Uptime, and ntfy handle chat, incidents, or notifications. The gap is an inexpensive review queue for low-urgency signed events with no paging model.
smallest_useful_product: Self-hosted receiver with endpoint aliases, event fingerprints, searchable timeline, acknowledge/archive state, daily digest, and JSON/CSV export. Non-goals: webhook retries, workflow automation, incident paging, or a Slack replacement.
success_measure: A pilot routes at least five sources through it and reduces unread operational Slack messages by 50% while retaining a searchable record for 30 days.
constraints: Verify signatures where supported; redact configured headers/body paths; provide retention deletion and a simple Docker deployment.
why_distinct: It is a calm audit inbox for informational events, not a quiet-hours rule engine or a generic webhook proxy.

title: Async Trace Stitcher
user: An engineer debugging one failed customer transaction across their app, queues, webhooks, and vendors who needs a defensible timeline without deploying a full tracing platform.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker describes manually reconstructing failed requests across logs, traces, dashboards, Stripe, Twilio, queues, and webhooks, and asks where manual stitching still breaks down.
A Grafana user reports that a Loki-to-correlation link only appears after adding a derived field, illustrating how cross-signal navigation is brittle even when the telemetry exists.

recurrence: Two independent production-debugging reports in 2025–26; severity is high when a customer-facing asynchronous flow has no single request path.
current_workaround: Open several vendor consoles, search each by request ID, paste timestamps into a document, and manually infer causality.
incumbents_and_gap: Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana Tempo, Jaeger, and Sentry provide tracing once instrumentation and propagation are complete. Small teams still need a low-setup, case-by-case stitcher for partial identifiers and exported evidence.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app that accepts redacted JSON/NDJSON exports from logs and webhooks, correlates configured IDs and timestamps, displays a proposed timeline with confidence, and exports a shareable incident bundle. Non-goals: ingesting live telemetry, replacing an APM, or making causal claims from no evidence.
success_measure: On five real incidents, an engineer produces a reviewable cross-system timeline in under 15 minutes and can identify every unmatched event explicitly.
constraints: Keep uploads in-browser by default; require visible correlation rules; scrub PII before export and never send vendor credentials.
why_distinct: It packages a one-off investigation from imperfect evidence rather than selling another always-on tracing backend.

title: Event Payload Spillway
user: A self-hosting developer whose automation or event system receives occasional large base64, media, or JSON payloads and needs to stop one bad event from filling the primary database.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker asks how to tier observability data because hot log storage is expensive and much of it is never queried after a short period.
A Windmill user reports that large base64 values in results create huge Postgres TOAST tables and fill disk space quickly.

recurrence: The same storage-growth pattern appears in log retention and workflow results; severity becomes acute when a shared Postgres disk fills.
current_workaround: Raise storage limits, manually delete records, cap payloads blindly, or build one-off object-storage code into each workflow.
incumbents_and_gap: S3 lifecycle rules, Loki retention, and application-specific blob stores exist. They do not give small self-hosted event systems a drop-in, content-aware spill decision with a readable stub and expiry plan.
smallest_useful_product: A reverse-proxy/library pair that detects configured oversized fields, writes the original encrypted payload to S3-compatible storage, replaces it with a signed reference and preview, and exposes expiry/reclaim reports. Non-goals: a general blob CDN, durable queue, or log analytics system.
success_measure: A test workload with large payloads keeps database growth below 10% of raw payload volume while operators can retrieve a referenced payload within two clicks.
constraints: Do not spill secrets without explicit allowlists; support local MinIO/S3-compatible stores; preserve webhook signatures before transformation and document retention/legal holds.
why_distinct: It is a narrow payload-overflow control, not a replacement for an event system, database, or observability store.

title: SQLite Sync Guard
user: A developer synchronizing folders between devices who needs an unambiguous warning and a safe export path before live SQLite/WAL files are copied or corrupted.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Syncthing user wants the same Firefox/database-backed profile on multiple machines but has learned that file-level database sync can corrupt data and cause loss.
A Syncthing user reports intermittent SQLITE_BUSY that stops a folder and asks for better handling, showing SQLite failure modes remain operationally visible.

recurrence: Two independent users in 2025–26 report SQLite and file-sync hazards; severity is high because the failure mode is corruption or a stopped sync folder.
current_workaround: Exclude the database, close the app before sync, hope WAL files are stable, or replace sync with a bespoke server database.
incumbents_and_gap: Syncthing warns users, SQLite has backup APIs, and Litestream/rqlite solve different replication problems. There is no small cross-platform preflight that recognizes unsafe sync sets and creates a consistent handoff artifact.
smallest_useful_product: CLI scans a configured sync root for SQLite DB/WAL/SHM files, detects active locks, explains risk, produces a consistent SQLite backup plus manifest, and writes ignore rules for supported sync clients. Non-goals: multi-writer SQLite replication, Firefox-profile merging, or a new sync service.
success_measure: On a fixture set of WAL and rollback-journal databases, it detects 100% of unsafe live sets and its exported backup passes sqlite3 integrity_check after transfer.
constraints: Never alter a live database without an explicit command; use SQLite's supported backup mechanisms; document that it prevents unsafe copying rather than enabling concurrent writes.
why_distinct: It makes existing file sync safer instead of claiming to solve distributed SQLite synchronization.

title: Restore Drill
user: A small team self-hosting Postgres and application data that needs recurring proof that a backup can restore into a usable isolated environment, not merely that a job completed.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Self-hosted Postgres users describe needing PITR, PgBouncer, replication, and observability but being stuck between SSH/scripts, Kubernetes operators, and enterprise products.
A user reports that restoring a backup into a fresh Appsmith instance leaves localhost unavailable, demonstrating that backup completion does not establish recoverability.

recurrence: Independent self-hosted operations request and a real restore failure in 2025; severity is existential when recovery is first attempted during an incident.
current_workaround: Trust backup logs, occasionally attempt a manual restore, or buy a managed database/PaaS.
incumbents_and_gap: restic, pgBackRest, WAL-G, and cloud backup products create backups; uptime monitors check production. The gap is a vendor-neutral scheduled restore rehearsal with application-level probes and a signed result.
smallest_useful_product: A Docker-first CLI that restores a chosen Postgres dump/volume into an isolated network, runs configurable SQL/HTTP smoke assertions, records duration and artifact hashes, then tears it down. Non-goals: backup storage, production restores, PITR orchestration, or general deployment management.
success_measure: A weekly drill succeeds unattended for four weeks and reports a measured recovery time; an intentionally broken backup is detected before the next scheduled drill.
constraints: Never target production endpoints; require an explicit disposable Docker network; protect dumps with local paths/credential files and securely delete temporary volumes where practical.
why_distinct: It verifies recovery rather than creating or hosting backups.

title: Secret Sync Preflight
user: A DevOps developer moving configuration through IaC, a secret manager, CI, and hosting providers who needs to detect missing, excess, stale, or provider-limited secrets before deployment.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A DevOps practitioner describes Terraform/Pulumi → Vault/KMS → CI → Kubernetes handoffs, copy-pasted credentials, and uncertainty about which layer owns truth.
A user asks for documentation of Supabase secret sync behavior at its hard 100-secret project limit, a concrete provider constraint that can turn sync into silent drift.

recurrence: Two independent configuration-chain reports in 2025–26; severity is high because a missing or wrongly deleted value can stop deployment or expose a secret.
current_workaround: Compare provider consoles by hand, keep an unreliable spreadsheet, or discover drift only when an application fails to start.
incumbents_and_gap: Vault, Infisical, Doppler, 1Password, Terraform, and secret operators each manage a layer. The gap is a read-only parity preflight across declared keys, destinations, limits, and deletion policy.
smallest_useful_product: CLI reads a key-only desired manifest and provider exports, highlights missing/extra/renamed keys, detects destination limits and dangerous delete plans, and emits CI annotations without reading values. Non-goals: storing or rotating secret values, replacing a secret manager, or automatic remediation.
success_measure: In a seeded multi-environment fixture, it catches all missing, extra, renamed, and over-limit key states without printing a secret value; a team blocks one unsafe deployment via CI.
constraints: Metadata-only by default; never log values; provider tokens must be least-privilege/read-only; treat key names as potentially sensitive and support local reports.
why_distinct: It is a cross-layer safety check, not another vault or an AI-generated configuration assistant.

title: Flag Removal Map
user: A lean engineering team that has shipped a feature flag and now needs a safe, evidence-based checklist to remove the flag and every code/config reference once the rollout is complete.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A feature-flag tool maker targets teams priced out of existing products and explicitly asks which lifecycle features matter, confirming small teams need simpler flag operations.
A Flagsmith user says stale flags are identified only by creation date and asks for last-evaluated time, showing the missing evidence needed to decide whether removal is safe.

recurrence: Independent 2025 requests expose both affordability and stale-flag evidence problems; severity grows with every rollout as flag debt obscures behavior.
current_workaround: Search the repository manually, rely on a flag provider's creation date, file a cleanup ticket, and hope no SDK/config reference remains.
incumbents_and_gap: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, and ConfigCat provide flag lifecycle views. They do not generally join provider evaluation evidence to static references across a small team's repositories and deployment manifests.
smallest_useful_product: CLI accepts a provider export and repositories, finds SDK/config references, records optional evaluation counts from a local export, classifies a flag as keep/remove/review, and creates a Markdown removal plan. Non-goals: serving flags, changing code automatically, or collecting user analytics.
success_measure: On a seeded monorepo, it finds 100% of known references and produces a removal checklist that lets a team delete one completed flag without a rollback.
constraints: Use provider read-only tokens or offline exports; support common SDK patterns conservatively; never infer that zero observed evaluations proves a flag is safe to remove.
why_distinct: It connects deployment evidence to code cleanup; it is not a feature-flag service.

title: Arazzo Proof Runner
user: An API owner experimenting with OpenAPI Arazzo who needs a small local runner that turns a multi-step workflow into a reproducible evidence report for tests and integration reviews.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants to auto-generate API tests from Arazzo workflows; a reply calls the lack of runners a chicken-and-egg problem.
A Bruno user says request-payload comparison would improve testing quality of life and blocks their use, showing a demand for comparing multi-case API evidence rather than just sending one request.

recurrence: An early-standard adopter explicitly identifies missing runners, with an independent API-client user requesting comparison-oriented request testing; the market is nascent but concrete.
current_workaround: Hand-write Postman/Bruno collections or scripts, run an experimental runner, and save request/response snippets manually.
incumbents_and_gap: Postman, Bruno, Hoppscotch, Schemathesis, and individual Arazzo experiments run HTTP calls. The gap is a transparent, local Arazzo subset runner that emits a stable proof artifact of steps, variable substitutions, assertions, and redacted diffs.
smallest_useful_product: CLI supports a documented Arazzo subset, executes against a selected environment, captures redacted request/response metadata and assertions, compares two runs, and writes a static HTML/JSON proof bundle. Non-goals: an API client GUI, LLM agent integration, cloud collaboration, or broad OpenAPI generation.
success_measure: Runs three representative multi-step Arazzo workflows deterministically in CI and makes a changed response assertion visible in a one-file report.
constraints: Never serialize authorization values; require an explicit environment file; track the evolving Arazzo specification and clearly label unsupported features.
why_distinct: It focuses on auditable workflow evidence for an under-served open standard, not another general API client.

title: Collector Pressure Lab
user: A self-hosting engineer running OpenTelemetry who needs to know whether a collector configuration will queue, shed, or overload under bursty telemetry before a production incident.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants a simple self-hosted metrics/traces setup rather than a cobbled Grafana stack and is already experimenting with OpenTelemetry tooling.
The Collector project proposes adaptive request concurrency for production exporters, acknowledging the need to operate safely under differing volume and latency conditions.

recurrence: A self-hosting operator asks for simpler observability while the Collector project is addressing production pressure control; severity is high when telemetry drops exactly during an incident.
current_workaround: Copy a Helm/Compose example, guess queue and batch settings, watch dashboards after deployment, then tune during overload.
incumbents_and_gap: OpenTelemetry Collector, Grafana Alloy, SigNoz, and vendor APMs ingest telemetry. They do not provide a small offline experiment that explains queue/backpressure consequences for a specific config and traffic sample.
smallest_useful_product: CLI loads a Collector config and a bounded OTLP/OTLP-like traffic sample, replays configurable bursts against a local collector, records queue/latency/drop behavior, and emits tuning hypotheses. Non-goals: an observability backend, a production traffic generator, or automatic config writes.
success_measure: For a controlled slow-exporter fixture, it correctly classifies backpressure versus drops and reports the threshold within 20% of measured throughput.
constraints: Default to loopback-only test endpoints; keep telemetry samples local; warn that synthetic results are not production capacity guarantees; honor OpenTelemetry component licenses.
why_distinct: It is a configuration pressure experiment, not a telemetry store or another Grafana distribution.

title: Migration Replay Gate
user: A team using schema snapshots and migrations that needs to replay an intended change against a disposable database and identify unsafe or non-idempotent operations before an environment apply fails.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker is evaluating continuous database alignment and explicitly asks about safety concerns of automated schema alignment and intentional environment divergence.
A Directus user reports that applying a schema diff tries to add an already-existing table/columns after snapshot behavior changed, a direct example of replay safety failing.

recurrence: A 2026 practitioner asks whether automated alignment is safe, while a 2025 schema-apply bug shows the operational risk; severity ranges from blocked deploys to destructive DDL.
current_workaround: Review generated SQL, run it manually in staging, trust a snapshot/diff tool, or avoid automated alignment altogether.
incumbents_and_gap: Flyway, Liquibase, Atlas, Prisma, Directus, and ORM migration tools manage migrations or snapshots. The gap is a CI-friendly replay gate that reports what actually happens when a proposed generated diff meets an already-partially-applied state.
smallest_useful_product: CLI starts a disposable Postgres database, seeds selected schema-state fixtures, applies a migration/diff command twice and after a partial state, captures SQL/errors, and labels non-idempotent/destructive outcomes. Non-goals: generating migrations, mutating shared staging/prod, row-data synchronization, or DB hosting.
success_measure: In a fixture suite with known duplicate-table, destructive, and clean changes, it correctly identifies each outcome and blocks the unsafe cases in CI.
constraints: Run only disposable containers; require user-supplied migration command; make destructive test fixtures explicit; never accept production connection strings.
why_distinct: It tests the behavior of a migration/diff tool under repeat and partial-state conditions rather than merely comparing schemas.

title: CSS Cause Map
user: A frontend developer diagnosing a live layout defect who needs a compact explanation of which CSS rule, ancestor, or dynamic DOM change caused an element's final size, offset, or gap.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker wants DevTools-aware help with questions such as why an element is not centered or what adds space below it, noting that editor context lacks the live DOM and dynamic CSS.

A Playwright user asks for trace-file extensibility because their tests include API, event-based, and mainframe flows, reflecting the need to add domain context to otherwise generic debugging artifacts.

recurrence: A direct browser-debugging request and a separate request to enrich debugging artifacts in 2025–26; layout diagnosis is frequent but individual incidents are short-lived.
current_workaround: Toggle rules in DevTools, inspect computed styles/box model manually, add temporary outlines, and compare screenshots or DOM snapshots.
incumbents_and_gap: Chrome/Firefox DevTools expose computed styles and box models; Chrome has AI assistance. The unresolved gap is a deterministic, shareable causal map that traces inherited layout constraints and captures the before/after proof without sending a page to a model.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension adds an element picker, captures computed layout plus ancestor constraints, ranks the CSS properties contributing to selected dimensions/offsets, and exports a scrubbed HTML/JSON report. Non-goals: editing CSS, visual regression testing, remote page inspection, or LLM diagnosis.
success_measure: On 20 seeded flex/grid/margin/position fixtures, the report names a contributing rule or ancestor for the target dimension in at least 18 cases, and a developer resolves a layout fixture without opening the full Styles pane.
constraints: Operate only on user-authorized tabs; do not transmit DOM content by default; clearly distinguish computed correlation from browser-layout causation; maintain Chrome extension permissions conservatively.
why_distinct: It produces deterministic causal evidence over a live DOM instead of adding a thin chat layer to DevTools.
